warnings.text: From 2055 (age 73) your savings and investments and pension can’t cover your spending. The gap is shown as an unfunded shortfall.
You haven’t chosen what to do with your leftover money, so the projection doesn’t save any of it (it’s treated as spent).

suggestions.title: Use your pension to avoid the 60% band
suggestions.text: Your adjusted net income is about £118,380. Between £100,000 and £125,140 you lose some personal allowance, so keep only about £20 of each extra £100. Paying £18,408 more a year into your pension (15.6% more of salary) brings it to £100,000 and saves about £12,787 tax a year.
howTo: Ask payroll or HR how to pay more into your workplace pension. Most schemes let you change it at any time.
If they offer salary sacrifice, ask about it: it saves National Insurance as well as tax.
Check your next payslip to see the new amount going in.

suggestions.title: Check for employer matching
suggestions.text: Your employer adds 3%. Many employers add more if you pay more — if yours does, that’s usually the best return available.

suggestions.title: Use your ISA allowance
suggestions.text: You have about £20,000 of this year’s £20,000 ISA allowance left. Growth and interest in an ISA are tax-free. For money you won’t need for at least five years, a stocks & shares ISA has historically beaten cash, but can fall in value.
howTo: Decide between a cash ISA and a stocks & shares ISA (for money you won’t need for at least five years).
Open one, or top up one you already have. The allowance runs from 6 April to 5 April.
Set up a monthly payment on payday so it happens without thinking about it.
